summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 and NEMO, which originally supported only IPv6, to register IPv4 addresses and prefixes and carry both IPv4 and IPv6 packets through the tunnel to the home agent. It also allows the mobile node to roam across IPv4-only networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A traveling device can keep both its old-style and new-style addresses and still be reached. This note makes that work through a tunnel back home.

subtitle: How a Mobile IPv6 device can hold IPv4 and IPv6 home addresses and roam over IPv4-only networks, even behind a NAT.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 and NEMO support IPv6 only, but mobile nodes are expected to need an IPv4 home address for a long time and may roam into networks that offer only IPv4, sometimes behind a NAT.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node registers IPv4 addresses and prefixes using new options in its Mobile IPv6 binding update, and tunnels IPv4 and IPv6 packets to its home agent in IPv6, IPv4 or UDP-over-IPv4, with NAT detection built into the binding update exchange.
tldr.outcome: One mobility protocol serves dual stack nodes in IPv6 and IPv4 networks, so there is no need to run two mobility protocols at once. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5555 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8553. It defines DSMIPv6, the dual stack extension of Mobile IPv6 and NEMO.

sections.title: Why Mobile IPv6 Needs Dual Stack Support
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) and NEMO (RFC 3963) let a mobile node move around the Internet while staying reachable at an IPv6 home address or prefix. The authors expect that mobile nodes will need an IPv4 home address for a long time, and that they will roam into networks that do not support IPv6 and so need an IPv4 care-of address.

This specification extends Mobile IPv6 so dual stack mobile nodes can ask their dual stack home agent to tunnel IPv4 and IPv6 packets addressed to their home addresses. A node then needs only Mobile IPv6 and NEMO, and does not need to run two mobility protocols at the same time. The RFC also covers mobile nodes in private IPv4 networks that must traverse a NAT to reach the home agent.

It considers five scenarios: an IPv4-only foreign network, a mobile node behind a NAT, a home agent behind a NAT, IPv4-only applications that need a stable IPv4 address, and networks that support both IPv6 and IPv4. For the last one, the mobile node should prefer an IPv6 care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine moving to a town that only speaks the old language, while you still want your mail to reach you. This RFC lets a traveling device keep getting mail in both old and new languages.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
The design needs three things: use IPv4 and IPv6 home or care-of addresses at the same time and tell the home agent about them, learn the home agent's IPv4 address as well as its IPv6 address, and detect and traverse a NAT.

Finding the home agent. The IPv6 anycast method of Mobile IPv6 does not work from an IPv4-only network, so the node learns the home agent's IPv4 address through DNS, either by name (with 'AAAA' and 'A' records) or by service using the SRV record from RFC 5026.

Binding management. If the foreign network supports IPv6, the node sends a binding update to the home agent's IPv6 address, optionally with the IPv4 home address option. The home agent creates two binding cache entries, one for each home address, both pointing at the IPv6 care-of address. If the foreign network offers only IPv4, the node tunnels the binding update to the home agent's IPv4 address and includes an IPv4 care-of address option. With public IPv4 addresses the tunnel is plain IPv4. With private addresses, IPv6 packets are tunneled using UDP and IPv4, and the UDP port allocated for the home agent is 4191.

Other points. Route optimization is not possible in IPv4-only networks or for IPv4 traffic, because of the difficulty of the return-routability test, so such traffic goes through the home agent. A node can ask for a dynamic IPv4 home address by sending 0.0.0.0 in the IPv4 home address option, and the binding lifetime is then bound to the minimum of the IPv6 binding lifetime and the IPv4 address lease time.
sections.plainLanguage: The traveling device calls its home base and says where it is now. The home base then forwards all its mail through a private tunnel, and if there is a gatekeeper in the way, the tunnel is wrapped in an extra envelope.

sections.title: New Options and a New Flag
sections.content:
The RFC adds four options to the Mobile IPv6 mobility header and one flag to the binding update. All options have an alignment requirement of 4n and a length value of 6.

  • IPv4 Home Address option (type 29): carries the prefix length, a P flag that requests a mobile network prefix, and the IPv4 home address. The value 0.0.0.0 asks the home agent to allocate an address. A prefix length of zero is invalid.
  • IPv4 Care-of Address option (type 32): carries the mobile node's IPv4 care-of address, used in an IPv4-only network.
  • IPv4 Address Acknowledgement option (type 30): sent in the binding acknowledgement with a status, the allocated prefix length and the IPv4 home address. Status values 0 to 127 mean success and higher values mean failure.
  • NAT Detection option (type 31): sent by the home agent to say a NAT was in the path. It has an F flag meaning UDP encapsulation is required and a refresh time in seconds. A refresh time of all 1s means keepalives are not needed.

The new F flag in the binding update requests UDP encapsulation whether or not a NAT is present. It SHOULD NOT be set when the node has an IPv6 care-of address, apart from the case in the care-of address selection rules.
sections.plainLanguage: These are new boxes on the form the traveler sends home: one for the old-style address, one for where they are right now, one for the home base's reply, and one that says whether a gatekeeper was spotted.

sections.title: Tunnelling Formats and Address Choice
sections.content:
A mobile node can tunnel IPv6 in IPv4, IPv4 in IPv6, or IPv6 in IPv6 as before, or use UDP encapsulation to tunnel IPv6 or IPv4 over IPv4. The UDP format is an IPv4 or IPv6 header, a UDP header, then the inner IP header and the rest. This format MUST be supported by all implementations and MUST always be used to send the binding update when in an IPv4-only network. Tunnel mode ESP can also be carried inside UDP, and the receiver tells whether ESP is present from the UDP port used.

When a dual stack network offers both address types, the node SHOULD prefer an IPv6 care-of address. If the binding update gets no answer, it resends using the exponential back-off of RFC 3775, and after three attempts in total without a binding acknowledgement it SHOULD send a new binding update using the IPv4 care-of address. The node is RECOMMENDED not to change address family on later moves unless it knows it has entered a different administrative domain. If packets are lost with IP-in-IP encapsulation over IPv4, for example because of firewall policy, the node may resend with the F flag set.

Tunnel changes can affect the link and path MTU. It is RECOMMENDED that ECN and DSCP information be copied between inner and outer headers, and the TTL must be decremented as with IP-in-IP encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The traveler tries the newest road first. If three tries get no answer, it takes the older road, and wraps its letters in an extra envelope if some roads block the usual kind.

sections.title: NAT Detection and Keepalives
sections.content:
NAT detection happens when the first binding update is sent. In an IPv4-only network the mobile node sends the binding update inside UDP and IPv4. The home agent compares the source address of the outer IPv4 header with the address in the IPv4 care-of address option. If they match, there was no NAT. If they differ, a NAT was in the path and the home agent adds the NAT detection option to the binding acknowledgement.

From then on, the binding acknowledgement and later packets are sent in UDP and IPv4 to the address and port seen in the binding update, which the home agent stores with the mobile node's tunnel. A mobile node MUST always tunnel binding updates in UDP in an IPv4-only network, which gives perpetual NAT detection. Without a NAT, packets use plain IPv4 unless the home agent forces UDP with the F flag.

To keep the NAT binding alive, an idle mobile node can send binding updates periodically. The default is NATKATIMEOUT, 110 seconds, and the node SHOULD use a different refresh time if the home agent suggests one. A node that only needs to start connections and does not need to be reachable does not have to refresh the binding. IKEv2 keepalives on UDP port 4500 are separate and are not handled by DSMIPv6 keepalives.
sections.plainLanguage: The home base checks whether the address on the envelope matches the address the traveler wrote inside. If not, someone in between rewrote it, so they know a gatekeeper is there. The traveler then pokes the gatekeeper every so often so the door stays open.

sections.title: Mobile Node and Home Agent Behavior
sections.content:
In an IPv4-only network the mobile node MUST wrap the binding update in UDP, use its IPv4 care-of address and the home agent's IPv4 address in the outer header, and use its IPv6 home address as the inner source. The packet MUST be authenticated as in RFC 3775. On a binding acknowledgement, the node creates one binding update list entry per home address that was accepted, and MUST tunnel in UDP and IPv4 if the NAT detection option is present. If the IPv4 acknowledgement is missing or reports failure, it creates only the IPv6 entry and MAY include the IPv4 option again later.

The home agent must act as a proxy for IPv4 address resolution for registered IPv4 home addresses, store the IPv4 home address that matches each IPv6 home address, and check that a supplied IPv4 address belongs to the mobile node. If an unspecified address is sent it SHOULD allocate one, and otherwise it MUST return status 132. If both addresses are accepted it creates a separate binding cache entry for each, and for an IPv4 care-of address it MUST set up a tunnel to it.

A node can remove only its IPv4 binding by sending a binding update without the IPv4 home address option. It cannot remove the IPv6 binding while keeping the IPv4 one, and a binding update with lifetime zero removes all bindings. Returning home while using IPv4 is not supported. Correspondent nodes are not affected by the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The traveler follows a checklist when writing home, and the home base follows its own checklist for handing out the old-style address. If either side says no, the traveler still keeps the new-style address.

sections.title: Security and IKE Interactions
sections.content:
A single binding update now covers both home addresses, but the IPsec security association is still based on the IPv6 home address. The home agent stores which IPv4 address belongs to which IPv6 address, so the IPv4 binding is as secure as the IPv6 one. IKEv2 is required as the default mechanism for dynamic keying. The binding update MUST be protected using ESP transport mode.

The NAT traversal here has the same weakness as RFC 3519: the outer IPv4 header is not authenticated, so a man in the middle who changes it could divert the mobile node's traffic to another receiver. Data traffic in an IPv4-only network uses tunnel mode ESP over port 4500 as in RFC 3948, with a separate child SA, and the mobile node MUST set up the SA over port 4500 if both sides support it, even without a NAT.

On a handover the home agent and mobile node must update their tunnel and IKE security associations with the new address and port. The mobile node can send an empty informational message when the K bit was set, can renegotiate the IKE SA, or MAY use MOBIKE (RFC 4555), which is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret handshake stays tied to the traveler's new-style identity, so the old-style address is protected too. The weak spot is the outer envelope, which anyone on the way could tamper with.
